name: Skin-only facelift
lead: A skin-only facelift is a form of rhytidectomy in which the surgeon lifts and redrapes the facial skin and removes the excess, without separately tightening or repositioning the deeper tissue layers such as the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) or facial muscles [1]. It is the older, simpler approach to facelifting and is contrasted in the surgical literature with SMAS, deep-plane and composite techniques [1].

Descriptions of the technique say it carries fewer complications and a faster recovery than deeper procedures, and that it may be suited to a simple jowl lift in patients in their 30s and 40s [1]. The same reference reports that skin-only results may last roughly 5 to 10 years, with some patients seeking a touch-up sooner [1]. No clinical trials of the technique specifically are present in the sources reviewed for this article, and the longevity figures come from an encyclopedia summary rather than from controlled studies.

paras: In a skin-only facelift only the skin is elevated and pulled; the SMAS and muscles are not mobilised. It may involve removing a simple ellipse of skin or raising a larger skin flap, and surgeons are described as needing skill to judge how much skin to remove and in which direction to pull [1]. Facelifts are usually performed under general anaesthesia or deep sedation and are often combined with eyelid surgery [1].

Facelift surgery between about 1900 and 1970 was essentially cutaneous: surgeons pulled the skin and cut away the excess, with the first reported facelift taking place in Berlin in 1901 [1]. SMAS-based techniques followed in the 1970s after Skoog introduced subfascial dissection and Mitz and Peyronie described the SMAS in 1976, and later deep-plane and volumetric approaches became widespread [1].

Facelift complications described in general include haematoma (the most common, usually within 24 hours), injury to the greater auricular or facial nerve branches, skin necrosis, scarring and, rarely, infection [1]. Smoking, hypertension and diabetes are listed as raising the risk of complications, and smoking is linked to a markedly higher rate of skin necrosis [1]. Excess skin removal or skin-tension-dependent closure can produce a so-called windswept appearance or displace the ears and earlobes [1].

timeline.event: First facelift reported in Berlin; skin-only techniques dominate until about 1970 [1].
Mitz and Peyronie describe the SMAS, shifting practice toward deeper-layer techniques [1].

card.summary: Lifting and trimming just the skin of the face; the oldest, simplest facelift, with milder recovery and a shorter-lived result than deeper techniques.
card.note: Surgical procedure; reported longevity figures come from summaries, not controlled trials.

quick.overview:
A skin-only facelift lifts the facial skin and removes the excess without working on the SMAS or muscle underneath. It was the standard facelift for most of the early 20th century and remains described as a simpler option for mild jowling.

Encyclopedia summaries say it has fewer complications and a faster recovery than deeper facelifts, but results are reported to last around 5 to 10 years. No dedicated trials were found.
quick.mechanism: The surgeon raises a skin flap, pulls it in a chosen direction, trims the surplus and closes the incision, relying on the skin itself to hold the result [1].
quick.risks: General facelift risks include haematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and infection; smoking, hypertension and diabetes raise risk. Skin-only technique is described as having fewer complications than deeper variants, but excessive skin tension can distort the ears or give a windswept look [1].
